claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) continues to show no improvement in survival rates.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) continues to show no improvement in survival rates.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract without specific data or citation provided in this sentence.

claim: PDAC has elevated ATP levels.
source: One aspect of PDAC is elevated ATP levels, pointing to the purinergic axis as a potential attractive therapeutic target.
evidence: Referenced later in the manuscript with citation to Hu et al., 2019.

claim: The purinergic axis plays essential roles in fibrosis, inflammation response, and immune function.
source: Mediated in part by highly druggable extracellular proteins, this axis plays essential roles in fibrosis, inflammation response, and immune function.
evidence: This is a general statement about the purinergic axis supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: P2RY2 presents as the purinergic gene with the strongest association with hypoxia.
source: P2RY2 presents as the purinergic gene with the strongest association with hypoxia, the highest cancer cell-specific expression, and the strongest impact on overall survival.
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic analysis of TCGA data presented in the manuscript.

claim: P2RY2 has the highest cancer cell-specific expression among purinergic genes.
source: P2RY2 presents as the purinergic gene with the strongest association with hypoxia, the highest cancer cell-specific expression, and the strongest impact on overall survival.
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic analysis and deconvolution data presented in the manuscript.

claim: P2RY2 has the strongest impact on overall survival among purinergic genes.
source: P2RY2 presents as the purinergic gene with the strongest association with hypoxia, the highest cancer cell-specific expression, and the strongest impact on overall survival.
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of TCGA data.

claim: P2Y2 is critical in facilitating invasion driven by extracellular ATP.
source: Invasion assays using a 3D spheroid model revealed P2Y2 to be critical in facilitating invasion driven by extracellular ATP.
evidence: Demonstrated through 3D spheroid invasion assays with ATP stimulation.

claim: ATP-driven invasion requires direct protein-protein interactions between P2Y2 and αV integrins.
source: Using genetic modification and pharmacological strategies, we demonstrate mechanistically that this ATP-driven invasion requires direct protein-protein interactions between P2Y2 and αV integrins.
evidence: Demonstrated through genetic modification, pharmacological inhibition, and super-resolution microscopy.

claim: P2Y2 regulates the amount and distribution of integrin αV in the plasma membrane.
source: DNA-PAINT super-resolution fluorescence microscopy reveals that P2Y2 regulates the amount and distribution of integrin αV in the plasma membrane.
evidence: Demonstrated through DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy experiments.

claim: Receptor-integrin interactions were required for effective downstream signaling, leading to cancer cell invasion.
source: Moreover, receptor-integrin interactions were required for effective downstream signaling, leading to cancer cell invasion.
evidence: Demonstrated through western blot analysis of FAK and ERK phosphorylation and invasion assays.

claim: PDAC accounts for 90% of diagnosed pancreatic cancer cases.
source: PDAC, which accounts for 90% of diagnosed pancreatic cancer cases, has the lowest survival rate of all common solid malignancies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PDAC epidemiology.

claim: PDAC has the lowest survival rate of all common solid malignancies.
source: PDAC, which accounts for 90% of diagnosed pancreatic cancer cases, has the lowest survival rate of all common solid malignancies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PDAC prognosis.

claim: More than 80% of PDAC patients present with unresectable tumors.
source: Surgery is the only potentially curative treatment, yet more than 80% of patients present with unresectable tumors (Kocher, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kocher, 2023.

claim: Most PDAC patients survive less than six months after diagnosis.
source: Consequently, most patients survive less than six months after diagnosis, resulting in a five year survival rate of less than 5% when accounting for all disease stages (Bengtsson et al., 2020; Kocher, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bengtsson et al., 2020 and Kocher, 2023.

claim: PDAC has a five year survival rate of less than 5% when accounting for all disease stages.
source: Consequently, most patients survive less than six months after diagnosis, resulting in a five year survival rate of less than 5% when accounting for all disease stages (Bengtsson et al., 2020; Kocher, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bengtsson et al., 2020 and Kocher, 2023.

claim: PDAC survival statistics have improved minimally in the past 50 years.
source: Despite continued efforts, this statistic has improved minimally in the past 50 years.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PDAC prognosis trends.

claim: Pancreatic cancer is predicted to be the second most common cause of cancer-related deaths by 2040.
source: Due to increasing incidence, late detection, and lack of effective therapies, pancreatic cancer is predicted to be the second most common cause of cancer-related deaths by 2040 (Rahib et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rahib et al., 2021.

claim: Failure to significantly improve clinical management of PDAC is mainly a result of chemoresistance.
source: Failure to significantly improve clinical management is mainly a result of chemoresistance (Neuzillet et al., 2017), thus it is of vital importance to find new therapeutics that can improve patient survival.
evidence: Supported by citation to Neuzillet et al., 2017.

claim: PDAC is characterized by its desmoplastic stroma, with dense fibrosis leading to impaired vascularisation and high levels of hypoxia.
source: PDAC is characterized by its desmoplastic stroma, with dense fibrosis leading to impaired vascularisation and high levels of hypoxia (Koong et al., 2000; Di Maggio, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koong et al., 2000 and Di Maggio, 2016.

claim: Lack of oxygen leads to cellular stress and death, resulting in the release of purines such as ATP and adenosine into the tumor microenvironment.
source: Lack of oxygen leads to cellular stress and death, resulting in the release of purines such as ATP and adenosine into the tumor microenvironment (Forrester and Williams, 1977; Pellegatti et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Forrester and Williams, 1977 and Pellegatti et al., 2008.

claim: Extracellular ATP concentration in PDAC is 200-fold more than in normal tissue.
source: Extracellular ATP concentration in PDAC is 200-fold more than in normal tissue (Hu et al., 2019), suggesting that purinergic signaling could represent an effective therapeutic target in pancreatic cancer.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2019.

claim: The proteins underpinning purinergic signaling comprise several highly druggable membrane proteins involved in the regulation of extracellular purines, mainly ATP and adenosine.
source: The proteins underpinning purinergic signaling comprise several highly druggable membrane proteins involved in the regulation of extracellular purines, mainly ATP and adenosine (Burnstock and Novak, 2012; Boison and Yegutkin, 2019; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burnstock and Novak, 2012; Boison and Yegutkin, 2019; Yu et al., 2021.

claim: Extracellular ATP is known to promote inflammation.
source: Extracellular ATP is known to promote inflammation (Kurashima et al., 2012), growth (Ko et al., 2012), and cell movement (Martínez-Ramírez et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kurashima et al., 2012.

claim: Extracellular ATP is known to promote growth.
source: Extracellular ATP is known to promote inflammation (Kurashima et al., 2012), growth (Ko et al., 2012), and cell movement (Martínez-Ramírez et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ko et al., 2012.

claim: Extracellular ATP is known to promote cell movement.
source: Extracellular ATP is known to promote inflammation (Kurashima et al., 2012), growth (Ko et al., 2012), and cell movement (Martínez-Ramírez et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martínez-Ramírez et al., 2016.

claim: Adenosine is anti-inflammatory and promotes immunosuppression.
source: Contrastingly, adenosine is anti-inflammatory and promotes immunosuppression (Schneider et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schneider et al., 2021.

claim: There are ongoing clinical trials in several cancers, including PDAC, for drugs targeting the ectonucleotidase CD73 and adenosine receptor 2 A in combination with PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors and/or chemotherapy.
source: There are ongoing clinical trials in several cancers, including PDAC, for drugs targeting the ectonucleotidase CD73 (NCT03454451, NCT03454451) and adenosine receptor 2 A (NCT03454451) in combination with PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors and/or chemotherapy.
evidence: Supported by clinical trial identifiers.

claim: A Phase II multi-cancer study evaluating an anti-CD73 and anti-PD-L1 combination was withdrawn due to minimal overall clinical activity.
source: However, a Phase II multi-cancer study evaluating an anti-CD73 and anti-PD-L1 combination was withdrawn due to minimal overall clinical activity (NCT04262388).
evidence: Supported by clinical trial identifier NCT04262388.

claim: The extracellular purinome encompasses 23 main surface proteins, including pannexin 1, P2X ion channels, ectonucleotidases, and the P2Y, and adenosine GPCRs.
source: The extracellular purinome encompasses 23 main surface proteins, including pannexin 1, P2X ion channels, ectonucleotidases, and the P2Y, and adenosine GPCRs (Di Virgilio et al., 2018; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Di Virgilio et al., 2018 and Figure 1A.

claim: High P2RY2 expression is associated with the highest hazard ratio (2.99, 95%, CI: 1.69–5.31, log-rank p=8.5 × 10–5) among purinergic genes in PDAC.
source: Expression of five purinergic genes correlated with decreased patient survival, with high P2RY2 expression being associated with the highest hazard ratio (2.99, 95%, CI: 1.69–5.31, log-rank p=8.5 × 10–5).
evidence: Supported by analysis of PAAD TCGA database shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Few genetic alterations in purinergic genes are observed in 0–3% of PDAC tumors.
source: Using cBioPortal (Gao, 2013), we generated OncoPrints of purinergic signaling genes from PAAD TCGA samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), observing few genetic alterations in 0–3% of tumors and a heterogeneous percentage of tumors with high mRNA expression (z-score >1) for each purinergic gene.
evidence: Supported by OncoPrint analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Most purinergic genes are related to the immunogenic subtype in the Bailey model, except for NT5E, ADORA2B, PANX1, and P2RY2, which are related to squamous.
source: In the Bailey model, most genes were related to the immunogenic subtype except for NT5E, ADORA2B, PANX1, and P2RY2, which are related to squamous (Bailey et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bailey et al., 2016 and analysis presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Collisson molecular subtyping showed several purinergic genes associated mostly with quasimesenchymal and exocrine subtypes.
source: Collisson molecular subtyping showed several purinergic genes associated mostly with quasimesenchymal and exocrine subtypes (Collisson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collisson et al., 2011 and analysis presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: ADA, NT5E, P2RY6, P2RY2, and PANX1 are associated with the Basal subtype in the Moffitt classification.
source: The Moffitt subtypes were not strongly associated with purinergic genes except for ADA, NT5E, P2RY6, P2RY2, and PANX1 associated with the Basal subtype (Moffitt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moffitt et al., 2015 and analysis presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: PDAC is known for its hypoxic environment, which is associated with worse overall survival (p=0.002).
source: PDAC is known for its hypoxic environment (Koong et al., 2000; Yuen and Díaz, 2014), which is associated with worse overall survival (p=0.002, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B); hypoxia can lead to cellular stress and death, resulting in the increase of extracellular purines (Forrester and Williams, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koong et al., 2000; Yuen and Díaz, 2014; Forrester and Williams, 1977 and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CD73 (NT5E), adenosine A2B receptor (ADORA2B), and P2Y2 (P2RY2) mRNA expression associated strongly with the high hypoxia score group for all three hypoxia scores (log2 ratio >0.5, FDR < 0.0001).
source: CD73 (NT5E), adenosine A2B receptor (ADORA2B), and P2Y2 (P2RY2) mRNA expression associated strongly with the high hypoxia score group for all three hypoxia scores (log2 ratio >0.5, FDR < 0.0001).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: P2Y2 had the highest log2 ratio in all hypoxia signatures compared to other purinergic genes.
source: P2Y2 had the highest log2 ratio in all hypoxia signatures compared to other purinergic genes.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Most genes related to high Winter hypoxia scores (P2RY2, ADORA2B, and NT5E) were expressed in the tumor epithelial tissue.
source: Mining published RNA-seq data from 60 paired PDAC samples of stroma and tumor microdissections (GSE93326) (Maurer et al., 2019) and performing differential expression analysis, we observed that most genes related to high Winter hypoxia scores (P2RY2, ADORA2B, and NT5E) were expressed in the tumor epithelial tissue (Figure 1D), except for PANX1, encoding for pannexin 1, which is involved in cellular ATP release (Bao et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by analysis of GSE93326 data from Maurer et al., 2019 and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PANX1 is expressed in stromal tissue rather than tumor epithelial tissue.
source: Mining published RNA-seq data from 60 paired PDAC samples of stroma and tumor microdissections (GSE93326) (Maurer et al., 2019) and performing differential expression analysis, we observed that most genes related to high Winter hypoxia scores (P2RY2, ADORA2B, and NT5E) were expressed in the tumor epithelial tissue (Figure 1D), except for PANX1, encoding for pannexin 1, which is involved in cellular ATP release (Bao et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by analysis of GSE93326 data from Maurer et al., 2019 and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Pannexin 1 is involved in cellular ATP release.
source: Mining published RNA-seq data from 60 paired PDAC samples of stroma and tumor microdissections (GSE93326) (Maurer et al., 2019) and performing differential expression analysis, we observed that most genes related to high Winter hypoxia scores (P2RY2, ADORA2B, and NT5E) were expressed in the tumor epithelial tissue (Figure 1D), except for PANX1, encoding for pannexin 1, which is involved in cellular ATP release (Bao et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bao et al., 2004.

claim: P2RY2 is the purinergic gene most highly associated with cancer cell-specific expression.
source: P2RY2, encoding P2Y2 - a GPCR activated by ATP and UTP, was shown to be the purinergic gene most highly associated with cancer cell-specific expression in all our independent analyses (Figure 1D and E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Supported by multiple independent analyses shown in Figure 1D, E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: P2Y2 is a GPCR activated by ATP and UTP.
source: P2RY2, encoding P2Y2 - a GPCR activated by ATP and UTP, was shown to be the purinergic gene most highly associated with cancer cell-specific expression in all our independent analyses (Figure 1D and E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is established knowledge about P2Y2 receptor pharmacology.

claim: P2RY2 showed the strongest correlation with all hypoxia scores.
source: P2RY2 additionally showed the strongest correlation with all hypoxia scores (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: P2RY2 expression had the biggest adverse impact on patient survival among purinergic genes.
source: Most importantly, of all purinergic genes, P2RY2 expression had the biggest adverse impact on patient survival (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: P2Y2 mRNA expression is localized to the epithelial tumor cell compartment and not stroma, normal epithelium, or endocrine tissues.
source: To validate our bioinformatic findings, based on microdissections from a 60 patient cohort (GSE93326) and from the deconvolution of 177 PAAD tissues from the TCGA, we performed RNAscope on human PDAC samples. This corroborated P2Y2 mRNA expression as being localized to the epithelial tumor cell compartment and not stroma, normal epithelium, or endocrine tissues (n=3, representative images of 2 different patients shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), matching our findings from larger publicly available cohorts, including P2Y2 IHC data from 264 patients in the Renji cohort (Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and citation to Hu et al., 2019.

claim: Tumor samples expressed significantly higher (p<0.0001) P2Y2 mRNA levels compared to the normal pancreas.
source: Using GEPIA (Tang et al., 2017), we analyzed PAAD TCGA and GTEx mRNA expression of tumor (n=179) and normal samples (n=171). Tumor samples expressed significantly higher (p<0.0001) P2Y2 mRNA levels compared to the normal pancreas (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by GEPIA analysis shown in Figure 2B and citation to Tang et al., 2017.

claim: High P2Y2 mRNA expression is associated with significantly decreased median overall survival in PDAC patients (median survival: 67.87 vs 17.27 months).
source: Kaplan-Meier analysis from PAAD TCGA KMplot (Lánczky and Győrffy, 2021) showed a significant decrease in median overall survival in patients with high P2Y2 mRNA expression (median survival: 67.87 vs 17.27 months) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figure 2C and citation to Lánczky and Győrffy, 2021.

claim: The top gene set enriched in the PANTHER pathway database for high P2Y2 expression in both PAAD TCGA and PDAC CPTAC cohorts was the 'integrin signaling pathway'.
source: To predict P2Y2 function in PDAC, we performed gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of high vs low mRNA expressing P2Y2 tumor samples, divided by the median expression, for PAAD TCGA (n=177) and the PDAC Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) (n=140) databases. The top gene set enriched in the PANTHER pathway database in both cohorts was the 'integrin signaling pathway' (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The top four enriched gene sets from the Gene Ontology 'Molecular function' functional database for high P2Y2 expression were associated with cell adhesion molecule binding, the cytoskeleton, protease binding, and extracellular matrix binding.
source: The top four enriched gene sets from the Gene Ontology 'Molecular function' functional database were associated with cell adhesion molecule binding, the cytoskeleton, protease binding, and extracellular matrix binding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: AsPC-1 cells treated with ATP (100 µM) showed cytoskeletal rearrangements which were blocked by the selective P2Y2 antagonist AR-C118925XX (AR-C; 5 µM).
source: As preliminary validation of the GSEA results in vitro, we used the PDAC cell line AsPC-1, transduced with Lifeact, a peptide that fluorescently labels filamentous actin structures (Riedl et al., 2008), and monitored cell morphology using the Incucyte live-cell analysis system. Cells treated with ATP (100 µM) showed cytoskeletal rearrangements which were blocked by the selective P2Y2 antagonist AR-C118925XX (AR-C; 5 µM; Figure 2E; Muoboghare et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by Incucyte imaging shown in Figure 2E and citations to Riedl et al., 2008 and Muoboghare et al., 2019.

claim: Exposing cells to ATP at 100 µM resulted in the biggest change in cell area when testing six concentrations from 0.01 to 1000 µM.
source: Exposing cells to ATP at 100 µM resulted in the biggest change in cell area when testing six concentrations from 0.01 to 1000 µM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ATP-driven morphological changes were fully reversed at 5 µM AR-C, while AR-C on its own had no effect on cell morphology.
source: ATP-driven morphological changes were fully reversed at 5 X (5 µM) the IC50 of AR-C (1 µM), while AR-C on its own had no effect on cell morphology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by Incucyte imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: P2Y2 is the only P2Y GPCR possessing an RGD motif, located in the first extracellular loop.
source: P2Y2 is the only P2Y GPCR possessing an RGD motif, located in the first extracellular loop (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about P2Y2 structure shown in Figure 2F.

claim: P2Y2 has been shown to interact with αV integrins through its RGD motif.
source: P2Y2 has been shown to interact with αV integrins through this RGD motif (Erb et al., 2001), but the significance of this interaction has not been explored in cancer.
evidence: Supported by citation to Erb et al., 2001.

claim: Immunofluorescence showed colocalization of integrin αV and P2Y2 in the PDAC cell lines AsPC-1, BxPC-3, and CAPAN-2.
source: Immunofluorescence (IF) showed colocalization of integrin αV and P2Y2 in the PDAC cell lines AsPC-1 as well as PDAC cell lines with strong epithelial morphology, BxPC-3 and CAPAN-2, while MIA PaCa-2 cells showed low expression of both proteins, and PANC-1 showed high integrin αV and low P2Y2, matching CCLE data (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: Supported by IF imaging shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: MIA PaCa-2 cells showed low expression of both P2Y2 and integrin αV proteins.
source: Immunofluorescence (IF) showed colocalization of integrin αV and P2Y2 in the PDAC cell lines AsPC-1 as well as PDAC cell lines with strong epithelial morphology, BxPC-3 and CAPAN-2, while MIA PaCa-2 cells showed low expression of both proteins, and PANC-1 showed high integrin αV and low P2Y2, matching CCLE data (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: Supported by IF imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: PANC-1 cells showed high integrin αV and low P2Y2 expression.
source: Immunofluorescence (IF) showed colocalization of integrin αV and P2Y2 in the PDAC cell lines AsPC-1 as well as PDAC cell lines with strong epithelial morphology, BxPC-3 and CAPAN-2, while MIA PaCa-2 cells showed low expression of both proteins, and PANC-1 showed high integrin αV and low P2Y2, matching CCLE data (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: Supported by IF imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: Stellate cells are crucial for successful hanging drop sphere formation.
source: PDAC cell lines were combined with stellate cells in a ratio of 1:2 (Kadaba et al., 2013), using an immortalized stellate cell line, PS-1 (Froeling et al., 2009) to form spheres (Figure 3A), recapitulating the ratios of the two biggest cellular components in PDAC. Stellate cells are crucial for successful hanging drop sphere formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and cancer cell invasion (Murray et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and citations to Kadaba et al., 2013; Froeling et al., 2009; Murray et al., 2022.

claim: ATP (100 µM) increased invasion of AsPC-1 cells significantly compared to vehicle control (p<0.0001).
source: Given that extracellular ATP concentration in tumors is in the hundred micromolar range (Pellegatti et al., 2008), spheres were treated with P2Y2 agonists ATP and UTP (100 µM). Both nucleotides increased invasion of the PDAC cell line AsPC-1 significantly compared to vehicle control (p<0.0001 and p=0.0013, respectively), and this was blocked by the P2Y2 selective antagonist AR-C (5 µM, p=0.0237, and p=0.0133; Figure 3B and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3B, C and citation to Pellegatti et al., 2008.

claim: UTP (100 µM) increased invasion of AsPC-1 cells significantly compared to vehicle control (p=0.0013).
source: Given that extracellular ATP concentration in tumors is in the hundred micromolar range (Pellegatti et al., 2008), spheres were treated with P2Y2 agonists ATP and UTP (100 µM). Both nucleotides increased invasion of the PDAC cell line AsPC-1 significantly compared to vehicle control (p<0.0001 and p=0.0013, respectively), and this was blocked by the P2Y2 selective antagonist AR-C (5 µM, p=0.0237, and p=0.0133; Figure 3B and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3B, C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AR-C (5 µM) blocked ATP-driven invasion in AsPC-1 spheres (p=0.0237).
source: Given that extracellular ATP concentration in tumors is in the hundred micromolar range (Pellegatti et al., 2008), spheres were treated with P2Y2 agonists ATP and UTP (100 µM). Both nucleotides increased invasion of the PDAC cell line AsPC-1 significantly compared to vehicle control (p<0.0001 and p=0.0013, respectively), and this was blocked by the P2Y2 selective antagonist AR-C (5 µM, p=0.0237, and p=0.0133; Figure 3B and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3B, C.

claim: AR-C (5 µM) blocked UTP-driven invasion in AsPC-1 spheres (p=0.0133).
source: Given that extracellular ATP concentration in tumors is in the hundred micromolar range (Pellegatti et al., 2008), spheres were treated with P2Y2 agonists ATP and UTP (100 µM). Both nucleotides increased invasion of the PDAC cell line AsPC-1 significantly compared to vehicle control (p<0.0001 and p=0.0013, respectively), and this was blocked by the P2Y2 selective antagonist AR-C (5 µM, p=0.0237, and p=0.0133; Figure 3B and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treating spheres with AR-C on its own did not show significant effects on invasion.
source: Treating spheres with AR-C on its own did not show significant effects on invasion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A non-hydrolyzable ATP (ATPγS;100 µM) showed similar effects to ATP on invasion.
source: Importantly, a non-hydrolyzable ATP (ATPγS;100 µM) showed similar effects to ATP, implicating ATP and not its metabolites as the cause of the invasion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PS-1 stellate cells showed negligible expression of P2Y2.
source: Of note, IF staining of PS-1 cells showed negligible expression of P2Y2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by IF imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: cRGDfV treatment reduced ATP-driven motility significantly in 3D spheroid invasion assays (p<0.0001).
source: To determine whether integrin association was necessary for ATP-driven invasion, we treated spheres with 10 µM cyclic RGDfV peptide (cRGDfV), which binds predominantly to αVβ3 to block integrin binding to RGD motifs (Kapp et al., 2017), such as that in P2Y2 (Ibuka et al., 2015). cRGDfV treatment reduced ATP-driven motility significantly, both in 3D spheroid invasion assays (p<0.0001) (Figure 3B and C) and in 2D Incucyte migration assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F) as did treatment with AR-C.
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3B, C and citations to Kapp et al., 2017 and Ibuka et al., 2015.

claim: cRGDfV binds predominantly to αVβ3 to block integrin binding to RGD motifs.
source: To determine whether integrin association was necessary for ATP-driven invasion, we treated spheres with 10 µM cyclic RGDfV peptide (cRGDfV), which binds predominantly to αVβ3 to block integrin binding to RGD motifs (Kapp et al., 2017), such as that in P2Y2 (Ibuka et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kapp et al., 2017 and Ibuka et al., 2015.

claim: cRGDfV treatment reduced ATP-driven motility in 2D Incucyte migration assays.
source: cRGDfV treatment reduced ATP-driven motility significantly, both in 3D spheroid invasion assays (p<0.0001) (Figure 3B and C) and in 2D Incucyte migration assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F) as did treatment with AR-C.
evidence: Supported by Incucyte migration assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: BxPC-3 cells showed similar ATP-driven invasion behavior to AsPC-1 cells.
source: To ensure that this behavior was not restricted to AsPC-1 cells, experiments were corroborated in the epithelial-like BxPC-3 cell line (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H; Tan et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H and citation to Tan et al., 1986.

claim: Silencing P2Y2 expression in AsPC-1 cells using siRNA abrogated the invasive response to ATP (p<0.0001).
source: To further verify that ATP-driven invasion was dependent on P2Y2, we silenced P2Y2 expression in AsPC-1 cells using siRNA (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), abrogating the invasive response to ATP (p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3D and siRNA validation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: AsPC-1 P2Y2CRISPR cells displayed a significant decrease in invasion compared to CTRCRISPR cells in both ATP-treated (p<0.0001) and non-treated (p=0.0005) conditions.
source: P2Y2 involvement in this phenomenon was confirmed by generating a P2Y2 CRISPR-Cas9 AsPC-1 cell line (P2Y2CRISPR), which displayed a significant decrease in invasion compared to a control guide RNA CRISPR cell line (CTRCRISPR) in both ATP-treated (p<0.0001) and non-treated (p=0.0005) conditions (Figure 3F and E).
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3E, F.

claim: AR-C showed no significant off-target effects in AsPC-1 P2Y2CRISPR spheres.
source: Additionally, we tested the off-target effects of AR-C in AsPC-1 P2Y2CRISPR spheres and confirmed no significant difference in invasion compared to the control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The RGD motif of P2Y2 is essential for ATP-driven cancer cell invasion.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that P2Y2 is essential for ATP-driven cancer cell invasion. To determine the importance of the RGD motif of P2Y2 in ATP-driven invasion, we obtained a mutant P2Y2 construct, where the RGD motif was replaced by RGE (P2Y2RGE), which has less affinity for αV integrins (Erb et al., 2001).
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental results with siRNA, CRISPR, and RGE mutant.

claim: The P2Y2RGE mutant has less affinity for αV integrins than wild-type P2Y2.
source: To determine the importance of the RGD motif of P2Y2 in ATP-driven invasion, we obtained a mutant P2Y2 construct, where the RGD motif was replaced by RGE (P2Y2RGE), which has less affinity for αV integrins (Erb et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Erb et al., 2001.

claim: Only AsPC-1 P2Y2CRISPR spheres containing P2Y2RGD transfected cells demonstrated a rescue of the ATP-driven invasive phenotype (p<0.0001).
source: This mutant was transfected into AsPC-1 P2Y2CRISPR cells and compared to cells transfected with wild-type P2Y2 (P2Y2RGD; Figure 3—figure supplement 1K). Only spheres containing P2Y2RGD transfected cells demonstrated a rescue of the ATP-driven invasive phenotype (p<0.0001; Figure 3G and H), with P2Y2RGE spheres not responding to ATP treatment.
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3G, H.

claim: P2Y2RGE spheres did not respond to ATP treatment.
source: This mutant was transfected into AsPC-1 P2Y2CRISPR cells and compared to cells transfected with wild-type P2Y2 (P2Y2RGD; Figure 3—figure supplement 1K). Only spheres containing P2Y2RGD transfected cells demonstrated a rescue of the ATP-driven invasive phenotype (p<0.0001; Figure 3G and H), with P2Y2RGE spheres not responding to ATP treatment.
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3G, H.

claim: No ATP-driven invasion was observed in PANC-1 cells transfected with an empty vector or with P2Y2RGE.
source: To ensure this behavior was not influenced by off-target CRISPR effects, we repeated the experiment in PANC-1 cell line, which expresses very low levels of P2Y2, but high levels of integrin αV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G). No ATP-driven invasion was observed in PANC-1 cells transfected with an empty vector (EV) or with P2Y2RGE (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3I, J.

claim: Only PANC-1 cells transfected with P2Y2RGD showed ATP-driven invasion (p<0.0001).
source: Only when transfecting PANC-1 cells with P2Y2RGD was ATP-driven invasion observed (p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid invasion assay data shown in Figure 3I, J.

claim: The RGD motif of P2Y2 is required for ATP-driven cancer cell invasion.
source: These results demonstrate that the RGD motif of P2Y2 is required for ATP-driven cancer cell invasion.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the collective experimental results with P2Y2RGD and P2Y2RGE mutants.

claim: The density of P2Y2 proteins at the membrane decreased by 42% when P2Y2RGD cells were treated with ATP, compared to control (p<0.0001).
source: We imaged AsPC-1 P2Y2CRISPR cells transfected with P2Y2RGD or P2Y2RGE in the absence or presence of 100 µM ATP for 1 hr (Figure 4D), observing a 42% decrease in the median density of P2Y2 proteins at the membrane when P2Y2RGD cells were treated with ATP, compared to control (p<0.0001; Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4D, E.

claim: A slight decrease in the density of P2Y2 proteins on P2Y2RGE cells following ATP treatment was not statistically significant (p=0.1570).
source: In contrast, although a slight decrease in the density of P2Y2 proteins on P2Y2RGE cells was observed following ATP treatment, this was not statistically significant (p=0.1570).
evidence: Supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The density of P2Y2 proteins and protein clusters in both P2Y2RGD and P2Y2RGE controls were equivalent (p>0.9999).
source: The density of P2Y2 proteins and protein clusters in both P2Y2RGD and P2Y2RGE controls were equivalent (Figure 4E and F; p>0.9999), indicating similar expression of the receptor at the surface in both control conditions.
evidence: Supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4E, F.

claim: The density of P2Y2 clusters decreased significantly in both P2Y2RGD and P2Y2RGE conditions when treated with ATP (43% decrease, p<0.0001 for P2Y2RGD, and 48% decrease, p=0.0002 for P2Y2RGE).
source: Interestingly, the density of P2Y2 clusters decreased significantly in both conditions when treated with ATP (Figure 4F; 43% decrease, p<0.0001 for P2Y2RGD, and 48% decrease, p=0.0002 for P2Y2RGE).
evidence: Supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ATP treatment of normal AsPC-1 cells resulted in a 68% decrease in P2Y2 at the membrane (p<0.0001), while co-treatment with cRGDfV prevented this change (p>0.9999).
source: We repeated these studies with normal AsPC-1 cells (untransfected and with unaltered P2Y2 expression) treated with ATP +/-cRGDfV, only observing a reduction of P2Y2 at the membrane with ATP alone (68% decrease, p<0.0001), while co-treatment with cRGDfV prevented this change (p>0.9999; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The RGD motif is required for αV integrin to control P2Y2 levels at the membrane.
source: These findings highlight that the RGD motif is required for αV integrin to control P2Y2 levels at the membrane.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from DNA-PAINT experiments with P2Y2RGD, P2Y2RGE, and cRGDfV treatments.

claim: Stimulating P2Y2RGD with ATP increased the density of αV molecules and αV clusters at the membrane (p=0.0003).
source: Turning to αV integrins, we observed an increase in the density of αV molecules and αV clusters at the membrane when stimulating P2Y2RGD with ATP (165 αV molecules/ROI, IQR = 162.75; 6.5 αV clusters/ROI, IQR = 8.75) compared to P2Y2RGD without stimulation (58 αV molecules/ROI, IQR = 41; 2.5 αV clusters/ROI, IQR = 2; p=0.0003; Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4G, H.

claim: Normal AsPC-1 cells showed significantly more αV molecules and clusters following ATP stimulation (p=0.0382 and p=0.0349).
source: This phenomenon was also observed with normal AsPC-1 cells, with significantly more αV molecules and clusters (p=0.0382 and p=0.0349) detected following ATP stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: P2Y2RGE transfected cells exhibited more αV molecules and clusters at the membrane compared to P2Y2RGD cells in absence of stimulation (p=0.0003, p=0.0024, respectively).
source: In absence of stimulation, P2Y2RGE transfected cells exhibited more αV molecules and clusters at the membrane (182 αV molecules/ROI, IQR = 262.75; 9 αV clusters/ROI IQR = 14) compared to P2Y2RGD cells (p=0.0003, p=0.0024, respectively).
evidence: Supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4G, H.

claim: Treating P2Y2RGE cells with ATP did not result in significant changes in αV molecules and clusters (p=0.7086; p=0.1846).
source: However, treating P2Y2RGE cells with ATP did not result in significant changes in αV molecules and clusters (p=0.7086; p=0.1846).
evidence: Supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4G, H.

claim: The increase in the number of αV clusters was due to an increase in the number of αV proteins at the membrane.
source: When the number of clusters was normalized with the number of αV molecules, to obtain the percentage of αV in clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), there was no significant difference between conditions (p>0.9999), indicating that the increase in the number of αV clusters was due to an increase in the number of αV proteins at the membrane.
evidence: Supported by DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Activated P2Y2 has an RGD motif-dependent function in localizing integrin αV to the membrane.
source: Taken together, these data indicate an RGD motif-dependent function of activated P2Y2 in localizing integrin αV to the membrane.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from DNA-PAINT experiments showing differential αV localization with P2Y2RGD vs P2Y2RGE.

claim: A higher percentage of integrin αV proteins were in <50 nm proximity to P2Y2 in P2Y2RGD cells following ATP stimulation (103% increase, p=0.0143).
source: We detected a higher percentage of integrin αV proteins in <50 nm proximity to P2Y2 in P2Y2RGD cells following ATP stimulation (Figure 4I; 103% increase, p=0.0143).
evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis from DNA-PAINT data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: P2Y2RGE cells stimulated with ATP showed a 43% decrease (p=0.0101) in αV molecules in close proximity to P2Y2 in comparison to unstimulated cells.
source: In contrast, P2Y2RGE cells stimulated with ATP showed a 43% decrease (p=0.0101) in αV molecules in close proximity to P2Y2 in comparison to unstimulated cells.
evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis from DNA-PAINT data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: ATP-stimulated P2Y2RGD and unstimulated P2Y2RGE cells showed an increased percentage of αV proteins spaced at 20-100 nm range compared to untreated P2Y2RGD cells (98% increase with p=0.0132 and 89% increase with p=0.0181).
source: Analyzing the percentage of αV proteins with NND in the 20–100 nm range, we saw a similar pattern (Figure 4J). ATP-stimulated P2Y2RGD and unstimulated P2Y2RGE cells showed an increased percentage of αV proteins spaced at this range compared to untreated P2Y2RGD cells (98% increase with p=0.0132 and 89% increase with p=0.0181).
evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis from DNA-PAINT data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: No significant changes were observed in NND of <20 nm between αV proteins in any of the conditions.
source: No significant changes were observed in NND of <20 nm between αV proteins in any of the conditions (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis from DNA-PAINT data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: P2Y2RGD molecules were in significantly closer proximity to each other compared to P2Y2RGE in control and stimulated conditions (p<0.0001 and p=0.007).
source: In contrast, P2Y2RGD molecules were in significantly closer proximity to each other compared to P2Y2RGE in control and stimulated conditions (p<0.0001 and p=0.007) (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis from DNA-PAINT data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: There is a reciprocal interaction between αV integrin and P2Y2 receptors, where P2Y2 can alter integrin localization to the plasma membrane while αV integrins influence activated P2Y2 membrane localization.
source: In summary, our SMLM studies demonstrate a reciprocal interaction between αV integrin and P2Y2 receptors, where P2Y2 can alter integrin localization to the plasma membrane while αV integrins influence activated P2Y2 membrane localization.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the collective DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy experiments.

claim: AsPC-1 cells displayed a significant increase of FAK and ERK phosphorylation after 15 min of ATP stimulation, which was abrogated by concomitant targeting of P2Y2 with AR-C.
source: There is growing evidence of the importance of endosomal GPCR signaling and its potential relevance in disease and therapeutic opportunities (Calebiro and Godbole, 2018). As we identified the RGD motif in P2Y2 having a possible role in receptor internalization, integrin dynamics, and invasion, we proceeded to look at integrin signaling through phosphorylation of FAK (p-FAK) and ERK (p-ERK) from 0 to 1 hr after treating with 100 µM ATP. AsPC-1 cells displayed a significant increase of FAK and ERK phosphorylation after 15 min of ATP stimulation, which was abrogated by concomitant targeting of P2Y2 with AR-C (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A and citation to Calebiro and Godbole, 2018.

claim: Impairing the RGD motif function in P2Y2 with cRGDfV or by transfecting AsPC-1 P2Y2CRISPR cells with the P2Y2RGE mutant decreased p-FAK and p-ERK levels.
source: When impairing the RGD motif function in P2Y2 with cRGDfV or by transfecting AsPC-1 P2Y2CRISPR cells with the P2Y2RGE mutant, p-FAK, and p-ERK levels decreased (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B, C.

claim: Targeting the RGD motif in P2Y2 impairs receptor signaling and inhibits pancreatic cancer cell invasion.
source: Collectively, targeting the RGD motif in P2Y2 impairs receptor signaling and inhibits pancreatic cancer cell invasion.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the collective experimental results showing effects of RGD motif targeting on signaling and invasion.

claim: Purinergic signaling has been associated classically with hypoxia and immune function in cancer.
source: Purinergic signaling has been associated classically with hypoxia and immune function in cancer (Di Virgilio et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Di Virgilio et al., 2018.

claim: Hypoxia induces ATP release in cells, as first reported in rat heart cells.
source: One of the first reports of hypoxia-inducing ATP release in cells identified an increase of extracellular ATP in rat heart cells when kept in hypoxic conditions (Forrester and Williams, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citation to Forrester and Williams, 1977.

claim: PDAC is a highly hypoxic cancer, with high levels of ATP reported in the tumor interstitial fluid of human and mouse PDAC tissues compared to healthy tissues.
source: PDAC is a highly hypoxic cancer, with high levels of ATP reported in the tumor interstitial fluid of human and mouse PDAC tissues compared to healthy tissues (Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2019.

claim: Expression of most purinergic genes was associated predominantly with immune cells, immunogenic PDAC subtype, and low hypoxia scores.
source: Expression of most purinergic genes was associated predominantly with immune cells, immunogenic PDAC subtype, and low hypoxia scores (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1C, E.

claim: Expression of genes correlated with worse survival and hypoxia (PANX1, NT5E, ADORA2B, and P2RY2) was associated with tumor cells and the squamous PDAC subtype.
source: In contrast, expression of genes correlated with worse survival and hypoxia (PANX1, NT5E, ADORA2B, and P2RY2) was associated with tumor cells and the squamous PDAC subtype, correlating with hypoxia, inflammation, and worse prognosis (Bailey et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic analysis and citation to Bailey et al., 2016.

claim: The squamous PDAC subtype correlates with hypoxia, inflammation, and worse prognosis.
source: In contrast, expression of genes correlated with worse survival and hypoxia (PANX1, NT5E, ADORA2B, and P2RY2) was associated with tumor cells and the squamous PDAC subtype, correlating with hypoxia, inflammation, and worse prognosis (Bailey et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bailey et al., 2016.

claim: The adenosine A2B receptor requires larger agonist concentrations for activation compared to other receptors in the same family, such as adenosine A2A.
source: Adenosine A2B receptor requires larger agonist concentrations for activation compared to other receptors in the same family, such as adenosine A2A (Bruns et al., 1986; Xing et al., 2016), and receptor expression has been reported to increase when cells are subjected to hypoxia (Feoktistov et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bruns et al., 1986 and Xing et al., 2016.

claim: Adenosine A2B receptor expression has been reported to increase when cells are subjected to hypoxia.
source: Adenosine A2B receptor requires larger agonist concentrations for activation compared to other receptors in the same family, such as adenosine A2A (Bruns et al., 1986; Xing et al., 2016), and receptor expression has been reported to increase when cells are subjected to hypoxia (Feoktistov et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feoktistov et al., 2004.

claim: HIF-1α has been shown to upregulate A2B and P2Y2 expression in liver cancer.
source: Moreover, HIF-1α has been shown to upregulate A2B and P2Y2 expression in liver cancer (Tak et al., 2016; Kwon et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tak et al., 2016 and Kwon et al., 2019.

claim: P2Y2 activation with ATP led to elevated HIF-1α expression in PDAC.
source: These observations were supported by published immunohistochemical staining of 264 human PDAC samples, showing that P2Y2 localized predominantly in cancer cells in human PDAC and that P2Y2 activation with ATP led to elevated HIF-1α expression (Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2019.

claim: P2Y2 has been associated with cancer cell growth and glycolysis in PDAC.
source: P2Y2 has been associated with cancer cell growth and glycolysis in PDAC (Ko et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ko et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Combination treatment of subcutaneous xenografts of AsPC-1 or BxPC-3 cells with the P2Y2 antagonist AR-C together with gemcitabine significantly decreased tumor weight and resulted in increased survival compared to placebo or gemcitabine monotherapy control.
source: Combination treatment of subcutaneous xenografts of AsPC-1 or BxPC-3 cells with the P2Y2 antagonist AR-C together with gemcitabine significantly decreased tumor weight and resulted in increased survival compared to placebo or gemcitabine monotherapy control (Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2019.

claim: Increased glycolysis and cytoskeletal rearrangements have been linked.
source: Increased glycolysis and cytoskeletal rearrangements have been linked (Park et al., 2020), and both events could occur downstream of P2Y2 activation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2020.

claim: P2Y2 has been implicated in invasive phenotypes in prostate, breast, and ovarian cancer.
source: P2Y2 has been implicated in invasive phenotypes in prostate, breast, and ovarian cancer (Jin et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015; Martínez-Ramírez et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jin et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015; Martínez-Ramírez et al., 2016.

claim: The binding of P2Y2 to integrins via its RGD motif is necessary for tubule formation in epithelial intestinal cell line 3D models.
source: This interaction can exert phenotypic effects – for example, the binding of P2Y2 to integrins via its RGD motif is necessary for tubule formation in epithelial intestinal cell line 3D models (Ibuka et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ibuka et al., 2015.

claim: There are currently no clinically efficacious P2Y2 antagonists, with poor oral bioavailability and low selectivity being major issues.
source: Despite efforts, there are currently no clinically efficacious P2Y2 antagonists, with poor oral bioavailability and low selectivity being major issues (Neumann et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neumann et al., 2022.

claim: P2Y2 can be targeted by blocking its interaction with RGD-binding integrins, due to its dependence on integrins for its pro-invasive function.
source: Our findings demonstrate that P2Y2 can also be targeted by blocking its interaction with RGD-binding integrins, due to its dependence on integrins for its pro-invasive function.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing that blocking P2Y2-integrin interactions inhibits invasion.

claim: GPCR-integrin crosstalk is involved in many biological processes.
source: GPCR-integrin crosstalk is involved in many biological processes (Wang et al., 2005; Teoh et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2005 and Teoh et al., 2012.

claim: Only one study has directly examined the spatial distribution of integrins and GPCRs using IF analysis.
source: Only one study has directly examined the spatial distribution of integrins and GPCRs, however, this relied on IF analysis (Erb et al., 2001), where only changes in the micron scale will be perceived, hence losing information on the nanoscale distances and individual protein interactions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Erb et al., 2001.

claim: P2Y2 at the cell surface was reduced significantly after 1 hr of UTP stimulation.
source: Following ATP stimulation, the number of P2Y2 proteins at the plasma membrane decreased significantly after 1 hr, implying receptor internalization, in line with previous work showing P2Y2 at the cell surface was reduced significantly after 1 hr of UTP stimulation (Tulapurkar et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tulapurkar et al., 2005.

claim: Cytoskeletal rearrangements were required for P2Y2 clathrin-mediated internalization.
source: Of note, cytoskeletal rearrangements, which we have also observed upon ATP stimulation (Figure 2E), were required for P2Y2 clathrin-mediated internalization, and authors noted that P2Y2 was most likely in a complex with integrins and extracellular matrix-binding proteins.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2E and inference from cited literature.

claim: P2Y2 affecting cell surface redistribution of αV integrin has been reported, with αV integrin clusters observed after 5 min stimulation with UTP.
source: P2Y2 affecting cell surface redistribution of αV integrin has been reported, with αV integrin clusters observed after 5 min stimulation with UTP (Chorna et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chorna et al., 2007.

claim: By reducing the ability of integrins to bind to the RGD of P2Y2, through receptor internalization, RGE mutation or through cRGDfV treatment, there is less RGD-triggered integrin endocytosis, hence less integrin recycling and an increase of integrins at the cell surface.
source: We speculate that by reducing the ability of integrins to bind to the RGD of P2Y2, through receptor internalization, RGE mutation or through cRGDfV treatment, there is less RGD-triggered integrin endocytosis, hence less integrin recycling and an increase of integrins at the cell surface.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data.

claim: This is the first single-molecule super-resolution study to explore integrin and GPCR dynamics.
source: This is the first single-molecule super-resolution study to explore integrin and GPCR dynamics and to demonstrate a requirement for integrin-P2Y2 interactions in cancer cell invasion.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: This is the first study to demonstrate a requirement for integrin-P2Y2 interactions in cancer cell invasion.
source: This is the first single-molecule super-resolution study to explore integrin and GPCR dynamics and to demonstrate a requirement for integrin-P2Y2 interactions in cancer cell invasion.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: P2Y2, via its RGD motif, has a pivotal role in ATP-induced PDAC invasion by interacting with and regulating the number of αV integrins at the plasma membrane.
source: In summary, our study demonstrates that P2Y2, via its RGD motif, has a pivotal role in ATP-induced PDAC invasion by interacting with and regulating the number of αV integrins at the plasma membrane, revealing this critical axis as a promising therapeutic target.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: The P2Y2-integrin αV axis is a promising therapeutic target in PDAC.
source: In summary, our study demonstrates that P2Y2, via its RGD motif, has a pivotal role in ATP-induced PDAC invasion by interacting with and regulating the number of αV integrins at the plasma membrane, revealing this critical axis as a promising therapeutic target.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing the importance of this interaction in invasion.
